Several subsequent studies applied similar decomposition logic to specific facets of model evaluation \citep{dodge2020finetuning, henderson2018deep, magnusson2023reproducibility}. \citet{messing2026hidden} brought Generalizability theory into LLM evaluation, decomposing variance across five methodology facets on a single benchmark (judge identity: 43.8\%; see Positioning below for detailed comparison). \citet{madaan2024quantifying} proposed per-factor variance metrics for LLM evaluation benchmarks but did not cross factors simultaneously. \citet{blackwell2024towards} quantified uncertainty in benchmark scores, and \citet{qian2026benchmark} conducted systematic meta-evaluation of LLM benchmarks; \citet{burnell2023rethink} called for rethinking evaluation reporting standards in AI. On the methodology side, \citet{sclar2024formatting} and BrittleBench \citep{brittlebench2026} found 50--76\% accuracy swings from prompt formatting; \citet{hua2025flaw} showed that much of this sensitivity is an artifact of log-likelihood scoring (our generation-based protocol controls for this). \citet{pezeshkpour2024ordering}, \citet{bui2025seeds}, and \citet{biderman2024lessons} documented ordering, seed, and training sensitivity respectively.
